title: Ketiv and qere, and textual variation

objectives.can: Explain what ketiv and qere are, recognise the commonest Aramaic cases, and say which of the two the library's text prints.

explanation.summary: In some places the consonants written in the Hebrew and Aramaic Bible differ from the word the reading tradition tells the reader to say. The written form is the ketiv and the read form is the qere. The library's text prints the read form, so you will never see a ketiv form in it; you will meet some variant spellings, and this lesson shows how to read them.

sections.heading: What is written and what is read
body: Ketiv means 'what is written' and qere means 'what is read'. The consonants of the Bible were fixed in writing long before the vowel points were added. In a number of places the scribes who handed the text down read aloud a word different from the one on the page. They did not change the consonants. They kept the written word and recorded the word to be read.

In a printed Hebrew and Aramaic Bible the two are shown together. The consonants of the ketiv stand in the line of text with the vowel points of the qere, and the consonants of the qere stand in the margin. So the vowels printed on such a word do not belong to its written consonants: they belong to the word that is read. This is why a ketiv word in a printed Bible can look impossible as it stands.
Ketiv and qere are not a mistake and a correction. Both are old, and the tradition kept both on purpose. The terms are used for Hebrew and for Aramaic alike.

sections.heading: What the library prints
body: The library's word-by-word text of the Aramaic of the Bible prints the reading tradition: where the written and the read forms differ, it gives the qere. The analysis of each word, the headword and the English gloss are of the word as read. The texts hold no ketiv forms.

Three things follow. First, whatever you see in the exercises of this course is a form that is read. Second, another edition may print other consonants at a few places, and that is not a sign that either edition is wrong. Third, the library's analysis does not say which words have a ketiv. You cannot tell from the data alone whether a given word is such a place, and this course does not guess. The library's documentation notes that the whole-verse text elsewhere in the library may print the consonants as written, so the word reader and the verse text can differ at these places; the word reader follows the reading tradition.

sections.heading: Variant spellings you will meet
body: Grammarians list the same kinds of word among the places where the Aramaic chapters have a ketiv and qere: the second person singular pronoun, the endings of the second person of the verb, the endings of the third feminine plural, and plural endings. The edition shows these words in more than one spelling, and the table below shows real examples. They are given as spellings found in the text, not as a list of ketiv forms.

The pronoun 'you' (masculine singular) stands in Daniel 3:10 as אַנְתְּ and in Daniel 2:29 as אַנְתְּה. It is the same word with the same meaning. The second person singular of the perfect shows four spellings of its ending: שָׂמְתָּ in Daniel 3:10, עֲבַדְתְּ in Daniel 4:32, חֲזַיְתָ in Daniel 2:45 and חֲזַיְתָה in Daniel 2:41. All four are 'you' (masculine singular), perfect.

The third feminine plural is rare. The texts have three such verbs: the perfect נְפַקָה in Daniel 5:5, where fingers 'came forth', the perfect וּנְפַלָה in Daniel 7:20, and the imperfect לֶהֶוְיָן in Daniel 5:17, where the king is told 'let your gifts be' for yourself. In the first the feminine plural shows in the ending -ָה, in the third in the ending -ָן. The feminine plural noun אֶצְבְּעָן, 'fingers', and the feminine plural participle וְכָתְבָן, 'and writing', in Daniel 5:5 also end in -ָן.

sections.heading: Other kinds of textual variation
body: Ketiv and qere are variation inside the Masoretic Text, the one text this course reads. Variation also exists between texts. Two Greek forms of Daniel survive, the Old Greek and the version called Theodotion's. In the Aramaic chapters 3 to 6 they differ from each other, and from the Aramaic text, at length. This is a fact about the manuscripts. The library reads the Aramaic of the Masoretic Text and does not rebuild a text from the Greek.

A reader who meets a difference between editions should therefore ask what kind it is. A different spelling of the same word is usually a matter of ketiv and qere or of printing. A different sentence is a matter for textual criticism, which weighs manuscripts and translations, and which is outside this course.

sections.heading: Reading with this in mind
body: When you meet a spelling that looks strange, take three steps. Look the word up in the library's analysis, which treats it as the word that is read. Compare it with the other spellings of the same word, as the table above does. Then learn it as a variant of a word you know, rather than as a new word.

The pronoun 'you' and the second person perfect are the places to practise, since they occur often and show several spellings. In the reading passage, Daniel 3:10–12 has the pronoun and perfect forms of the second person addressed to the king.

misunderstandings: Ketiv is not a mistake and qere is not a correction made by a modern editor. They are two old recorded forms of one place, kept side by side by the tradition.
The vowels on a ketiv word in a printed Bible are those of the qere. Do not try to read the written consonants with them as if they belonged together.
This library does not show both. It prints the qere, and its analysis does not mark which words have a ketiv, so an unusual spelling is not on that account a ketiv.
A difference between two editions is not always a ketiv-qere place. It may be a different manuscript, a different reading of a printed text or a misprint.

deeper.heading: Why the tradition kept both
body: The scribes who copied the text held that the consonants were to be handed on exactly as they had received them. Where the reading they knew differed from the written word, they did not alter the text: they added a note. The result is that a printed Bible keeps both traditions, the written one in the line and the spoken one in the margin.

practice.prompt: What does the word ketiv mean?
options: what is written: the consonants on the page
practice.explain: Ketiv means 'what is written'. What is read aloud is the qere. A vowel sign is a point, and neither term is a note about accents.

practice.prompt: At a place where the written form and the read form differ, what does the library's word-by-word text print?
options: neither: the word is left out
the form that is written, the ketiv
the form that is read, the qere
practice.explain: The library follows the reading tradition and prints the qere. It does not print both, and it does not leave the word out.

check.prompt: In a printed Bible, whose vowel points does a ketiv word carry?
options: the vowels of the written consonants
the vowels of the next word
the vowels of the qere, the word that is read
check.explain: The vowels printed on a ketiv word belong to the qere. This is why the word can look impossible as printed. The other readings do not describe the practice.

check.prompt: Which statement about the reading tradition and the written consonants is right?
options: it removed the words that were read differently
it replaced the consonants with the read form
it added the qere to the text and left the vowels out
it left the consonants as written and recorded the word to be read
check.explain: The scribes kept the consonants and recorded the word to be read. They did not change the text or delete words.

check.prompt: You open another printed edition and find different consonants for a word in the library's Aramaic text. Which explanation should you consider first?
options: the word is from another language
the other edition prints the written form (ketiv) where the library prints the read form (qere)
the library has made a mistake
check.explain: Where the written and read forms differ, the library prints the read form, and another edition may print the written one. A difference is not on that account a mistake, though other causes, such as a misprint, are possible.

check.prompt: Which statement about the Greek forms of Daniel is correct?
options: the Greek forms are the ketiv
the Old Greek and Theodotion's version differ from each other, and from the Aramaic, at length in chapters 3 to 6; the library reads the Aramaic only
the library rebuilds the Aramaic from the Greek
only one Greek form exists, and it agrees with the Aramaic word for word
check.explain: Two Greek forms of Daniel survive and they differ at length in the Aramaic chapters. This is a fact about the manuscripts. It is not the same thing as ketiv and qere, and the library does not reconstruct a text from the Greek.
